title: Security Evidence Toolkit · Handbook · Scutoria
main: Back to the toolkit PDF Scutoria · Security Evidence Toolkit · Handbook Version 23 October 2026 Security Evidence Toolkit · Handbook Why every question is asked, which source stands behind it, and what a small business can honestly show Sources read at the originals on 19 October 2026; corrected passages checked again on 23 October 2026 0 How to use this toolkit The toolkit turns the answers to forty-seven questions into seven dated documents. This handbook explains why each question is asked, which source stands behind it, which answer a questionnaire, an insurer or a contract clause actually wants, and what a business without an IT department can honestly show. You do not need to read it before you start. Every question in the generator names the section that explains it. The seven documents. D1 the security self-declaration: nine sections A to I, one overview table, every field with its status and date, signed by the management; it is the document you attach to a questionnaire. D2 the action plan: every "partly" and "not yet" becomes a measure with a priority, a responsible person, a target date in one of three waves and the evidence that exists afterwards; as a sheet with a review tab. D3 the emergency card: one page for the wall and the drawer. D4 the evidence list: per question the proof a customer or insurer accepts, whether it exists, where it is, its attachment number. D5 the cover letter with the questionnaire mapping: the letter that names the gaps with their dates, and the table that maps the typical questions of a questionnaire and the ten areas of Article 21(2) of the NIS 2 Directive to the sections of the self-declaration. D6 the clause checklist: the security clauses customers write into contracts, what each means, what a small business can promise and what it should negotiate. D7 the evidence summary: one dated page with a document number. The four answers. Every status question has four answers: in place, partly, not yet with a date, not applicable with a reason. "Not yet, by the end of the quarter" is a complete answer. A questionnaire that gets it learns more than from a "yes" that falls apart at the first follow-up question, and the law that covers your customer expects exactly this of the customer itself: whoever finds a gap takes corrective measures without undue delay (section 1.7). The toolkit never writes "all requirements met", "secure", or a deadline you cannot keep. What the toolkit is not. It is not legal advice, not an audit and not a certificate. No document claims that the business complies with a law or a standard. The documents show what the business has in place on a given date, what it will do by when, and who answers for it. Where a source is missing, the handbook says so and leaves the decision with the business. The four markers. Every statement that matters carries one of four markers. Fact: wording or date read at the original source, which is named with its retrieval date. Interpretation: a conclusion Scutoria draws from the sources; it can be argued with. Uncertain: the sources contradict each other or the legal situation is open; the handbook says what was checked and when. Gap: no source answers the question; the business decides and the document leaves the field open on purpose. The example business. The generator is prefilled with a fictional electrical contractor with ten to forty-nine staff in Austria, whose IT is looked after partly by an external provider and partly by the office. A customer has sent a questionnaire. The example answers show a realistic mixed picture: multi-factor authentication on email yes, on the cloud console not yet; a daily backup, but no copy out of reach; a restore never tested; no emergency plan; an old workshop computer. No person and no business in this handbook is real. The order of work. Answer the questions; about forty minutes. Read D1 and the action plan. Print the emergency card and check its numbers. Create the evidence that already exists in an hour (section 3). Send the self-declaration with the cover letter, or file it for the insurer. Work through the first wave of the plan. Review on the date in D7. 1 Why you are asked Four kinds of requests arrive at small businesses: a questionnaire from a larger customer, a contract with security clauses, an application form of a cyber insurer, and the wish to show a label or a certificate. This section says where each comes from and why the size of the business sets the measure. 1.1 Customers under the NIS 2 Directive Fact The NIS 2 Directive applies to public or private entities of a type listed in its Annex I or II which qualify as medium-sized enterprises under the Commission's SME Recommendation or exceed those ceilings, with exceptions regardless of size in Article 2(2). Medium-sized means fifty persons or more, or a turnover and a balance sheet total both above ten million euro, up to 249 persons and fifty or forty-three million euro. The figures of partner and linked enterprises count as well (Annex, Art. 3 and 6), so a small business owned by a larger group may be covered. The sectors include energy, transport, banking, health, water, digital infrastructure, managed IT services, public administration, space, postal services, waste, chemicals, food, the manufacturing of medical devices, computers, electrical equipment, machinery and vehicles, digital providers and research. Source: Directive (EU) 2022/2555 , Art. 2(1) and (2), Annexes I and II · EUR-Lex · retrieved 2026-10-19; Commission Recommendation 2003/361/EC , Annex, Art. 2, 3 and 6 · retrieved 2026-10-23 Fact Such entities must take "appropriate and proportionate technical, operational and organisational measures". The measures must include at least ten areas, among them "supply chain security, including security-related aspects concerning the relationships between each entity and its direct suppliers or service providers". When deciding which supply chain measures are appropriate, entities "take into account the vulnerabilities specific to each direct supplier and service provider and the overall quality of products and cybersecurity practices of their suppliers and service providers, including their secure development procedures". Source: Directive (EU) 2022/2555 , Art. 21(1), (2)(d) and (3) · EUR-Lex · retrieved 2026-10-19 Interpretation This is the questionnaire. The Directive does not tell the customer what to ask a supplier; it obliges the customer to consider the supplier's practices, and a questionnaire is the cheapest way to do that for hundreds of suppliers at once. The questions therefore follow the customer's own ten areas, and the self-declaration follows the questions. The Directive and the national laws that transpose it bind the customer, not you. What binds you is the contract that follows (section 1.2 and D6) and, wherever you handle personal data, the GDPR itself: Article 32 requires every controller and processor to take appropriate technical and organisational measures, among them encryption, the ability to restore personal data in a timely manner after an incident, and a process for regularly testing the measures. Fact Under the GDPR "the controller and the processor shall implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk", including "the pseudonymisation and encryption of personal data", "the ability to restore the availability and access to personal data in a timely manner in the event of a physical or technical incident" and "a process for regularly testing, assessing and evaluating the effectiveness" of the measures. Source: Regulation (EU) 2016/679 , Art. 32(1)(a) to (d) · EUR-Lex · retrieved 2026-10-23 Fact The Directive is transposed by national law. In Germany the new BSI Act (BSI-Gesetz of 2 December 2025, enacted by the NIS 2 transposition act) has been in force since 6 December 2025. In Austria the Network and Information System Security Act 2026 (NISG 2026) has been in force in its core provisions since 1 October 2026; its § 32(4) repeats the ten areas, with supply chain security including the relationships with direct suppliers and service providers in point (d), and its § 33(1) requires essential and important entities to send the authority a structured self-declaration within twelve months of the registration duty arising, in particular on the network and information systems used and the security of the supply chains. Source: BSI-Gesetz of 2 December 2025, BGBl. 2025 I No. 301, last amended on 23 July 2026, BGBl. 2026 I No. 226 · gesetze-im-internet.de · retrieved 2026-10-23; NISG 2026, BGBl. I No. 94/2025 of 23 December 2025, § 32(4), § 33(1) · ris.bka.gv.at · retrieved 2026-10-19 Interpretation For an Austrian customer, the supplier questionnaire is the raw material of its own self-declaration. Whoever asks you in 2026 is collecting what it has to send to the authority in 2027. That explains the tone and the deadlines of the requests; it does not make your answers a filing with the authority. The self-declaration describes your business; the customer decides what it does with it. 1.2 The Implementing Regulation: the contract behind the questionnaire Fact For the providers named in Article 21(5) of the Directive (DNS, TLD registries, cloud, data centres, content delivery, managed and managed security services, online marketplaces, search engines, social networks, trust services; "digital providers" in this handbook) the Commission has laid down the technical requirements of the ten areas in Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2690, published in the Official Journal on 18 October 2024 and in force since 7 November 2024. Its Annex, point 5.1.4, says what such entities put into their contracts with suppliers "where appropriate": cybersecurity requirements; awareness, skills, training and, where appropriate, certifications required of the supplier's staff; background checks of the supplier's staff; an obligation to report incidents "without undue delay"; the right to audit or to receive audit reports; an obligation to handle vulnerabilities; requirements regarding subcontracting; and obligations upon termination of the contract, such as "retrieval and disposal" of the information obtained. Point 5.2 requires a directory of direct suppliers with contact points and a list of the products and services each supplies. Source: Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2690 of 17 October 2024, OJ L, 2024/2690, 18.10.2024, Art. 2(1), Art. 16, Annex points 5.1.4 and 5.2 · EUR-Lex, English and German · retrieved 2026-10-19 Fact In Austria the same Annex applies to every essential and important entity: the regulation of the cybersecurity authority of 1 October 2026 (NISV 2026) declares the requirements of Article 2 and the Annex of the Implementing Regulation applicable to the types of entities listed in Annexes 1 and 2 of the NISG 2026 that the Implementing Regulation itself does not cover. Source: NISV 2026 , BGBl. II No. 290/2026 of 1 October 2026, § 2 · ris.bka.gv.at · retrieved 2026-10-19 Interpretation So the eight contract contents of point 5.1.4 are the pattern of the clauses you will see: from digital providers across the Union, and from every NIS 2 customer in Austria. A German customer outside the digital sectors is not bound to the Annex by law, but its auditors and lawyers read the same text. D6 takes the eight contents one by one and says what a small business can promise. 1.3 Financial customers: DORA Fact Banks, insurers, investment firms and other financial entities fall under the Digital Operational Resilience Act. Its Article 30(2) lists nine contents that every contract on ICT services must contain, among them a description of the service including subcontracting, the locations of data processing and prior notice of their change, data protection provisions, access and return of data, service levels, assistance in incidents, cooperation with authorities and termination rights. Article 30(3) adds six for critical or important functions, among them full service levels, notice periods and reporting duties, contingency plans and security measures, participation in threat-led penetration testing, unrestricted access and audit rights, and exit strategies. Source: Regulation (EU) 2022/2554 (DORA), Art. 28(8), Art. 30(2) and (3) · EUR-Lex · retrieved 2026-10-19 Interpretation These contents are mandatory only where you provide ICT services to the financial entity: software, IT support, hosting, devices you operate for it. A supplier of goods or of services without ICT, such as an electrical installation, is not covered by Article 30, even if the bank sends the same clause set; it may say so and ask for the clauses to be removed. If you do provide ICT services, Part B of D6 explains each clause; the audit right of Article 30(3)(e) applies only where your service supports a critical or important function, and it is the one to negotiate. 1.4 Insurers Fact Six public documents of insurers were read in full: four application forms for cyber cover (Mannheimer, for businesses from 10 million euro turnover; Markel; Beazley; Funk with Beazley), one questionnaire for IT liability (Allianz) and one set of policy conditions (Donau). Most of them ask: backups on separate systems with a tested restore (Mannheimer 4.1, 4.2, 4.5, 4.6, 4.9; Markel section 4 point 5 and 7.2; Beazley critical requirement 1; Funk 1); multi-factor authentication for cloud services, email, remote access and administrators (Mannheimer 7.7.1, 7.7.3, 8.1; Markel 6.2; Allianz 2.5.5; Beazley 2 and 3); patches applied promptly and no software without manufacturer updates (Mannheimer 7.1; Markel 7.3, within four weeks, CVSS 8.0 or higher without delay; Allianz 2.5.1 and 2.5.3; Beazley and Funk 5); protective software on all devices with automatic updates (Mannheimer 7.2; Markel 7.3; Beazley; Funk 7); annual training with anti-phishing (Mannheimer 5.4; Markel 6.4; Beazley 4; Funk 4); a responsible person and a written emergency and recovery plan (Mannheimer 5.1, 5.10; Markel 6.3); administrator rights only for administration (Mannheimer 6.3, 6.5; Allianz 2.5.4); a process for granting and revoking access (Mannheimer 5.5); network segmentation (Mannheimer 7.4). Beazley calls four of these a mandatory condition for taking out cyber cover. The conditions of an Austrian insurer oblige the policyholder to use appropriate protective measures, in particular for backups, anti-virus software, password settings, authorisation concepts, system configuration, firewalls and software updates, to notify the insurer without undue delay and at the latest within one week of becoming aware, to call its hotline without undue delay, and cover private devices only where their access is subject to two-factor authentication. How often to back up varies: Markel asks for weekly backups below one million euro turnover and daily above, Beazley says monthly may be enough where little changes. Source: Mannheimer Versicherung AG , Fragebogen Cyber-Risiken für Unternehmen ab 10 Mio. Euro Umsatz, HF_060 0424; Markel Insurance SE , Fragebogen Pro Cyber v2; Allianz Versicherungs-AG , Fragebogen für Unternehmen der Informationstechnologie (IT-Haftpflicht), 9.25; Beazley, Sicherheitsanforderungen für die Cyber Versicherung, undated; Funk International Austria with Beazley, Antrag und Risikofragebogen, July 2022; Donau Versicherung AG, Allgemeine Bedingungen für die Cyberversicherung, Fassung 2025, Teil D 7.1.3 and 7.1.4, Teil E · retrieved 2026-10-23 Interpretation The insurers ask largely what the law makes customers ask, in plainer words and with numbers. Where the toolkit names a rhythm (daily, yearly, within days), it takes the strictest of the forms, because the self-declaration must hold in front of all of them. Where a form is stricter than the law, the handbook says so at the question. 1.5 Labels, checks and certificates Fact Austria has a label with four levels. The Cyber Trust Austria label is issued by CTS Cyber Trust Services GmbH; the underlying rating belongs to KSV1870 and the scheme to the Kompetenzzentrum Sicheres Österreich. The Standard level rests on a self-declaration against fourteen published questions (B1 to B14), validated by KSV1870; Silver and Gold add eleven questions (A1 to A11), Gold with an audit by a qualified body; Platinum rests on the fifty requirements into which the scheme divides the Implementing Regulation. The label is valid for one year. Its scheme policy, version 6.0 of 8 September 2025, publishes the questions; the website names suppliers of essential and important entities under the NISG 2026 as its target. Source: Cyber Trust Austria , Cyber Risk Rating & Cyber Trust Label Schema Policy 2026, version 6.0 of 8 September 2025, pp. 5 to 21; cyber-trust.at, label overview and B questions · retrieved 2026-10-19 Fact Germany has a check, not a certificate. The CyberRisikoCheck under DIN SPEC 27076:2023-05 is a one- to two-hour interview by a qualified IT service provider against 27 requirements in six areas, aimed at businesses with up to fifty staff; the BSI says it is not an IT security certification and does not establish NIS 2 conformity; the DIN SPEC is free after registration. The BSI qualified its thousandth provider on 6 June 2025 and reports that businesses met on average only just under 56 percent of the requirements. VdS 10000:2025-01 is a management standard for SMEs by the insurers' testing body, based on ISO 27001 and the BSI baseline, with certification valid for three years and reduced annual re-audits; insurer forms name it next to ISO 27001. Source: BSI, CyberRisikoCheck page and press release of 6 June 2025 ; BSI, Die Lage der IT-Sicherheit in Deutschland , section on SMEs; DIN Media, DIN SPEC 27076 ; VdS 10000 : 2025-01 (03), table of contents and preliminary remarks; VdS 5569 : 2018-10, pp. 5 and 9 · retrieved 2026-10-19 Fact ISO/IEC 27001:2022 is the international standard; its Annex A lists 93 controls in four themes, taken from ISO/IEC 27002:2022. The standard is paid (CHF 155, retrieved 2026-10-23; check the current price). TISAX is the assessment scheme of the automotive industry on the VDA ISA catalogue, operated by ENX, with three assessment levels and three-year validity. The SIG of Shared Assessments is a questionnaire library sold by subscription with 21 risk domains. Source: committee.iso.org and IEC Webstore, ISO/IEC 27001:2022 , edition 3; SC 27 Journal 2025, issue 1, pp. 10, 18 to 19; ENX Association, TISAX handbook and NIS2 fulfilment through TISAX , 24 April 2025; Shared Assessments, SIG · retrieved 2026-10-19 Interpretation For a business with ten to fifty staff, none of these is the first step, and most customers do not demand one. We searched for a customer or a tender that requires the Austrian label and found none; only press releases of label holders. The order that works: first the self-declaration with evidence (this toolkit), then, if a customer or insurer asks for an external check, the cheapest matching one: the CyberRisikoCheck in Germany, the Standard label in Austria; both cover much of blocks B to G. Question B3 records what you already have; D4 lists a certificate as an attachment, nothing more. 1.6 Why size sets the measure Fact The Directive itself ties the measures to size: "due account shall be taken of the degree of the entity's exposure to risks, the entity's size and the likelihood of occurrence of incidents and their severity". The Implementing Regulation repeats this for its Annex and adds that where the Annex qualifies a requirement with "where appropriate", "where applicable" or "to the extent feasible", an entity which considers it not appropriate, applicable or feasible documents its reasons; its recital 5 says micro entities that cannot segregate duties may rely on compensating measures such as targeted oversight by management or increased monitoring and logging. Austrian law repeats the test in § 32(3) NISG 2026, and its regulation obliges entities to document compensating measures and review them yearly. Source: Directive (EU) 2022/2555 , Art. 21(1) second subparagraph; Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2690 , Art. 2(2) second subparagraph and recital 5; NISG 2026 , § 32(3); NISV 2026 , § 4 · retrieved 2026-10-23 Interpretation Proportionality is written for the entity, not for its suppliers, and no law stops a customer from asking more of a supplier than of itself. But a customer that must justify its own measures by its size has a good reason to accept a small supplier's answers measured by the supplier's size, and you may say so. That is why the self-declaration opens with the size of the business (question A3) and why D5 says in its first paragraph that the answers are those of a small business. Nothing in the toolkit asks a small business for a security operations centre, penetration tests or a certification; those are the Silver and Gold questions of the label, not the Standard ones. 1.7 Why "not yet, with a date" is a complete answer Fact The Directive obliges an entity that finds it does not comply with the measures to take "without undue delay, all necessary, appropriate and proportionate corrective measures". The Implementing Regulation asks for compliance monitoring and regular reporting to the management bodies; Austria's § 33(3) expects an audit report with the identified deficiencies and an action plan to remedy them. Source: Directive (EU) 2022/2555 , Art. 21(4); Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2690 , Annex 2.2.1; NISG 2026 , § 33(3) · retrieved 2026-10-19 Fact Austria makes the point in its penalty provisions: failing to implement the measures of § 32 is an offence only insofar as the authority did not learn of it solely from the entity's self-declaration, while knowingly false statements in a self-declaration are an offence of their own. Source: NISG 2026 , § 45(1) point 3 and (4) point 8 · ris.bka.gv.at · retrieved 2026-10-23 Interpretation The law treats a documented gap with a plan as a normal state; Austria even spares the gap that an entity reports itself and punishes the false answer instead. A supplier that writes "not yet, planned by 31 March, responsible: the office manager with the IT provider" gives the customer what the customer must produce for itself. That is the whole reasoning behind the four answers and the action plan, and it is why D7 lists open points instead of hiding them. 2 The areas of the self-declaration Each area is one block of the questionnaire and one section of D1. For each question the handbook says what is asked, which source asks it, what a small business can realistically show, and what the example business answered. The emergency questions of block F are explained in section 4 as well. Quotations from German sources are our translations. 2.1 B · Organisation B1 Written security rules. One or two pages for staff: devices, passwords, email, payments, what to report and to whom. Fact The first question of the Austrian label is whether the business has a current information security policy that is valid for the company. The first of ENISA's twelve steps for SMEs is to develop a security culture, with "publish cybersecurity policies" among its sub-steps. The Implementing Regulation opens its Annex with the policy on the security of network and information systems; VdS 10000 devotes chapters 5 and 6 to the policy and the guidelines; Mannheimer asks for a responsible person. Source: Cyber Trust Austria , Schema Policy 2026, B1; ENISA, Cybersecurity guide for SMEs , 12 steps, 28 June 2021, step 1; Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2690 , Annex 1.1; VdS 10000 :2025-01, chapters 5 and 6; Mannheimer, 5.1 · retrieved 2026-10-19 Interpretation Two pages signed by the management and acknowledged by each person are enough for every questionnaire we read; nobody asks a ten-person business for a management system. The example business has rules for passwords and email but not for reporting: "partly", with the rules completed in the second wave. B2 Cyber insurance. Whether a policy exists, with insurer, emergency number and notification deadline. Interpretation No law requires a cyber insurance, and no questionnaire we read asks for it as a condition; the question stands because insurers' own forms, the label's question A9 (qualified resources in a serious incident, possibly through a cyber insurance) and the emergency card need the answer: the policy's emergency number and its notification deadline belong on the card. D1 reports the fact without judgement. The example business has no policy. Source: Cyber Trust Austria , Schema Policy 2026, A9; Donau Versicherung , AVB Cyber 2025, Teil D 7.1.4 · retrieved 2026-10-19 B3 Certificates, labels, checks. What the business already holds: ISO 27001, the Austrian label, TISAX, a CyberRisikoCheck, other. Fact Insurers ask for it: Allianz 1.2 lists ISO 27001 and VdS 10000; Mannheimer 5.3 asks whether the business runs regular analyses against ISO 27001, the BSI baseline or DIN SPEC 27076, and 9.2 whether the IT provider is certified. The Implementing Regulation asks relevant entities for an independent review of their security and for policies to assess effectiveness. Source: Allianz, 1.2; Mannheimer, 5.3 and 9.2; Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2690 , Annex 2.3 and 7 · retrieved 2026-10-19 Interpretation What exists becomes an attachment in D4; what does not exist is not a gap in the plan, because section 1.5 explains why a certificate is not the first step. The example business holds none. 2.2 C · Access and identity C1 One account per person. Fact Markel's form asks whether an individual user ID with password is assigned to every user and administrator. The Implementing Regulation requires identification of users and authentication; the BSI baseline module on identity and access management asks for individual accounts; TISAX control 4.1.3 asks how user accounts and login information are managed. Source: Markel, 6.2; Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2690 , Annex 11.5 and 11.6; BSI, IT-Grundschutz ORP.4 , edition 2023; ENX, NIS2 fulfilment through TISAX , control 4.1.3 · retrieved 2026-10-19 Interpretation Shared logins break every other control: you cannot revoke, log or attribute. Where a tool allows only one login, the measure in D2 keeps its password in the password manager with a named owner. The example business answered "in place". C2 Multi-factor authentication for every email account. Fact The insurers rank it among their few mandatory conditions: Beazley's critical requirement 2 and Funk's question 2 ask for multi-factor authentication for cloud-based services, with cloud-based email accounts as the example, and for all remote access. The Austrian label's B6 asks for appropriate authentication with the criterion that MFA must be in use at least for critical systems. The Implementing Regulation requires that users are authenticated "by multiple authentication factors or continuous authentication mechanisms", where appropriate and in accordance with the classification of the asset; the Directive names multi-factor authentication in Article 21(2)(j). ENISA's step 5 is "secure access to systems" with "enable multi-factor authentication"; the Austrian criminal police office lists MFA for email accounts first among the technical measures against CEO fraud. Source: Beazley, requirement 2; Funk, question 2; Cyber Trust Austria , Schema Policy 2026, B6; Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2690 , Annex 11.7.1; Directive (EU) 2022/2555 , Art. 21(2)(j); ENISA, 12 steps , step 5; Bundeskriminalamt, CEO Fraud , updated 29 June 2026 · retrieved 2026-10-19 Fact On the method: the US standard for digital identity treats phishing resistance as a property of the authentication protocol, and CISA ranks authenticator apps and security keys above codes by SMS, which it places last among MFA methods but still above a password alone. Source: NIST SP 800-63B-4 , July 2025, section 3.2.5 · retrieved 2026-10-23; CISA, Implementing Phishing-Resistant MFA , October 2022 · retrieved 2026-10-19 Interpretation That every mailbox is "critical" is our conclusion, not the label's wording: ENISA's SME report describes the compromised mailbox as the start of payment fraud, and one of the first things an attacker does with a mailbox is to reset passwords elsewhere. The example business has an authenticator app on every mailbox: "in place". C3 Multi-factor authentication for remote access, administrators, cloud consoles and online banking. Fact Mannheimer asks whether MFA is used for access to important systems, whether administrators necessarily need MFA for the internal servers and cloud structures, and whether home office access is possible only with MFA. Markel asks for MFA for remote access to all systems and for administrator access and, for larger businesses, allows remote access only with two-factor authentication or VPN. Allianz asks whether logins from outside the company network are possible only with MFA. Beazley's requirements 2 and 3: MFA for all remote access, no remote access without VPN. The label's A6 names MFA for all externally reachable systems such as VPN, jump hosts, remote support tools and webmail. The Implementing Regulation requires strong identification, authentication such as multi-factor authentication and authorisation procedures for privileged accounts and system administration accounts, and controls for remote access including access by service providers. The Austrian insurer covers private devices only where their access is subject to two-factor authentication. Source: Mannheimer, 7.7.1, 7.7.3, 8.1; Markel, section 4 point 6 and 6.2; Allianz, 2.5.5; Beazley, 2 and 3; Cyber Trust Austria , Schema Policy 2026, A6; Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2690 , Annex 11.3.2(a) and 6.7.2(d); Donau Versicherung , AVB Cyber 2025, Teil E · retrieved 2026-10-19 Interpretation Online banking is on the list because the bank already enforces a second factor and because the emergency card names the bank; no questionnaire asks for it. The example business: VPN yes, the administration console of the cloud not yet: "partly", first wave. C4 Accounts of leavers disabled on the day of leaving, from a list of all accounts. Fact Mannheimer asks whether a formal process for the assignment and revocation of access rights exists. The Implementing Regulation requires procedures for the termination or change of employment, the management of access rights and the return or deletion of assets upon termination; the label's B4 asks for a maintained directory of all IT assets and services including cloud services; ENISA's SME report lists revoking access when staff leave among its recommendations. Source: Mannheimer, 5.5; Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2690 , Annex 10.3, 11.2, 12.5; Cyber Trust Austria , Schema Policy 2026, B4; ENISA, Cybersecurity for SMEs , June 2021 · retrieved 2026-10-19 Interpretation "On the day of leaving" is our rule; the sources say "procedure". The list of all accounts per person is the evidence that makes the procedure possible, and it is the same list C1 needs. The example business has no written list: "partly". C5 Daily work without administrator rights, separate accounts for administration. Fact Mannheimer asks whether administrative access is reserved exclusively to administrators and exclusively for administrative tasks, and whether local administrator rights on clients were disabled; Allianz asks for differentiated admin rights; the label's B5 asks for an authorisation concept that grants only the rights necessary for the work. The Implementing Regulation requires dedicated accounts to be used exclusively for system administration operations and separate credentials for privileged or administrative accounts. Source: Mannheimer, 6.3 and 6.5; Allianz, 2.5.4; Cyber Trust Austria , Schema Policy 2026, B5; Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2690 , Annex 11.3.2(b) and 11.6.2(f) · retrieved 2026-10-19 Interpretation This is the one measure that costs nothing and keeps much malware from installing itself. The example business works with administrator rights on every machine: "not yet", second wave, with the IT provider. C6 Password rule: one long password per account in a password manager, changed only on suspicion. Fact The US standard requires at least fifteen characters where the password is the only factor and eight where a second factor is used, forbids composition rules and periodic change unless there is evidence of compromise, requires a check against blocklists of known passwords, and permits password managers. The BSI argued publicly against forced periodic changes on 31 January 2025 and 30 January 2026. The Austrian insurer's conditions name password settings among the obligations of the policyholder. Source: NIST SP 800-63B-4 , July 2025, sections 3.1.1.1 and 3.1.1.2; BSI press releases of 31 January 2025 and 30 January 2026 ; Donau Versicherung , AVB Cyber 2025, Teil D 7.1.3 · retrieved 2026-10-19 Uncertain The Implementing Regulation points the other way: it requires relevant entities to demand the change of authentication data at first use, at predefined intervals and whenever there is a suspicion that the data has been compromised, to block users after a predefined number of failed attempts, and to match the strength of authentication to the asset. Source: Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2690 , Annex 11.6.2(a), (c) and (d), English and German text · retrieved 2026-10-19 Uncertain Which password rule should a supplier promise? The standards bodies and the Commission's Implementing Regulation differ on periodic change. The toolkit follows NIST and the BSI: long, unique, in a manager, changed on suspicion, protected by a second factor. If a customer or an insurer insists on intervals and cites the Regulation, the honest answer is to agree an interval for accounts that have no second factor and to keep MFA everywhere else; D1 states which rule applies. ENISA's advisory guidance on the Implementing Regulation reads point 11.6.2 the toolkit's way: change passwords "as necessary, for example after a security incident", and use at least 8 characters with MFA and 14 without (ENISA, NIS2 Technical Implementation Guidance, June 2025, p. 142, retrieved 2026-10-23). No court or authority decision on this conflict was searched. Last checked 2026-10-23 · open point 6.17 Interpretation The example business has a manager for the office but not for field staff: "partly". 2.3 D · Backup and continuity D1 Daily automatic backup of all business data with one copy offline or otherwise out of an attacker's reach. Fact Most insurer forms ask about it: how often, whether the media are physically separated from the active systems, whether change or destruction of the backup is excluded, whether the backup system sits in the same directory service, whether a backup and recovery concept exists (Mannheimer 4.1, 4.5, 4.6, 4.7, 4.9); Markel requires backups on separated systems or media at least weekly below one million euro turnover and daily above; Beazley's first critical requirement is tested offline backups; Funk's question 1 asks for a cold or offline location that would not be affected by a problem with the live environment. The Implementing Regulation requires backup copies "in a safe location or locations, which are not in the same network as the system, and are at sufficient distance to escape any damage from a disaster at the main site". ENISA's step 9 is "secure backups"; the Directive's area (c) names backup management and disaster recovery. Source: Mannheimer, 4.1, 4.5, 4.6, 4.7, 4.9; Markel, section 4 point 5; Beazley, 1; Funk, 1; Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2690 , Annex 4.2.2(c); ENISA, 12 steps , step 9; Directive (EU) 2022/2555 , Art. 21(2)(c) · retrieved 2026-10-19; Regulation (EU) 2016/679 , Art. 32(1)(a), (c), (d) · retrieved 2026-10-23 Interpretation "Out of reach" is the whole point: a backup on a disk that is always connected, or in a cloud folder the office account can delete, is the next encrypted backup. Daily is the strictest rhythm in the forms and the one the toolkit asks. The example business backs up daily to a NAS in the office with no offline copy: "partly", first wave. D2 Restore tested in the last twelve months, with the duration noted. Fact Mannheimer asks for the date of the last successful restore test of critical systems; Markel asks whether all backups are restore-tested at least once a year; Beazley and Funk want backups tested regularly to make sure they can be restored. The Implementing Regulation requires regular testing of the recovery of backup copies and redundancies. Source: Mannheimer, 4.2; Markel, 7.2; Beazley, 1; Funk, 1; Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2690 , Annex 4.2.6 · retrieved 2026-10-19; Regulation (EU) 2016/679 , Art. 32(1)(a), (c), (d) · retrieved 2026-10-23 Interpretation Noting the duration is our addition; it shows whether the IT is back within the time the business can bridge (D3). One folder restored, time stopped, date and result on one line: that is the evidence. The example business has never tested: "not yet", first wave. D3 How long the business could keep working without its IT. Fact Mannheimer asks for an emergency and recovery concept; the Implementing Regulation requires backup plans to state recovery times and a business continuity plan with the order of recovery; VdS 10000 has a chapter on identifying critical IT resources and one on recovery plans; TISAX carries assessment objectives for high availability. Source: Mannheimer, 5.10; Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2690 , Annex 4.1.2 and 4.2.2(a); VdS 10000 :2025-01, chapters 9 and 17.5; ENX, NIS2 fulfilment through TISAX , table 1 · retrieved 2026-10-19 Interpretation The question is not graded; it sets priorities. A business that can bridge a week with paper and phones needs a different plan from one that stops within hours. The answer goes into section D of the self-declaration and onto the emergency card ("we can bridge"). The example business: one day. D4 A written emergency plan: whom to call, what to do first, in which order to restore. Fact The label's B14 asks whether the business has an emergency plan on the basis of which it reacts to an IT security incident, with the criterion that plans are tested at least every two years; Markel asks for an IT emergency plan that is fixed in writing and names responsible persons; Mannheimer for an emergency and recovery concept; ENISA's step 4 is "develop an incident response plan". The Implementing Regulation requires an incident handling policy with roles, responsibilities and procedures, and a business continuity plan with contact details, activation conditions and the order of recovery. Source: Cyber Trust Austria , Schema Policy 2026, B14; Markel, 6.3; Mannheimer, 5.10; ENISA, 12 steps , step 4; Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2690 , Annex 3.1.1 and 4.1.2 · retrieved 2026-10-19 Interpretation For a small business the emergency card is the plan: one page with the first hour, the numbers, the deadlines and where things are, modelled on the BSI's IT-Notfallkarte (section 4). Posting it and dating it is the evidence; a drill once a year, even at the desk, keeps it alive; the label's B14 wants a test at least every two years that includes restoring data and services, which is the restore test of D2. The example business has none: "not yet", first wave. 2.4 E · Updates and devices E1 Updates installed automatically within days on every computer, phone and server. Fact The label's B9 asks whether all IT systems and applications are regularly updated with security updates, with the criterion that no security update may be overdue for longer than one quarter. Markel asks whether security patches are installed within four weeks and critical ones with a CVSS score of 8.0 or higher without delay; Mannheimer asks for a patch management procedure for automatic or prompt installation; Allianz for a patch management that evaluates, prioritises and rolls out patches every working day; Beazley and Funk for critical patches as soon as possible. The Implementing Regulation requires that "security patches are applied within a reasonable time after they become available", tested before production, and from trusted sources. ENISA's step 6 begins with "keep software patched and up to date". Source: Cyber Trust Austria , Schema Policy 2026, B9; Markel, 7.3; Mannheimer, 7.1; Allianz, 2.5.3; Beazley; Funk, 5; Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2690 , Annex 6.6.1(a) to (c); ENISA, 12 steps , step 6 · retrieved 2026-10-19 Interpretation "Within days" is stricter than the label's quarter and Markel's four weeks; it is what automatic updates do on their own, and automatic is the only way a business without an IT department keeps up. A monthly check that they ran, noted on one line, is the evidence. The example business: "in place". E2 A list of all devices, and every device and program still supported by its manufacturer. Fact The label's B4 asks for a regularly maintained directory of all IT assets and services including cloud services; Markel excludes access to outdated systems without manufacturer security updates, naming Windows 7, XP and NT, unless they sit on a separate network; Allianz asks whether no software beyond its end-of-life date is in use; Beazley and Funk exclude end-of-support and end-of-life software. The Implementing Regulation requires "a complete, accurate, up-to-date and consistent inventory" of assets; the Directive's area (i) names asset management. Source: Cyber Trust Austria , Schema Policy 2026, B4; Markel, section 4 point 6; Allianz, 2.5.1; Beazley; Funk, 5; Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2690 , Annex 12.4.1; Directive (EU) 2022/2555 , Art. 21(2)(i) · retrieved 2026-10-19 Interpretation A device list of ten lines with a column "supported until" answers three questions at once: asset inventory, end of life, and who uses what. The example business has no written list and an old workshop computer: "partly", second wave; the computer leaves the network or gets replaced. E3 Protective software on every computer; laptops and phones encrypted. Fact Mannheimer asks whether all systems have protection against malware with automatic updates; Markel for an endpoint protection solution that updates automatically and for anti-virus with current databases; Beazley and Funk for anti-virus or endpoint protection on all devices and the scanning of incoming email. The label's B11 asks whether systems are monitored for malware and B12 whether sensitive data is encrypted in transit. The Implementing Regulation requires protection "against malicious and unauthorised software" and a cryptography policy; ENISA's step 6 lists anti-virus, email and web protection and encryption; the Directive's area (h) names cryptography and encryption. Source: Mannheimer, 7.2; Markel, section 4 point 5 and 7.3; Beazley; Funk, 6 and 7; Cyber Trust Austria , Schema Policy 2026, B11 and B12; Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2690 , Annex 6.9.1 and 9; ENISA, 12 steps , step 6; Directive (EU) 2022/2555 , Art. 21(2)(h) · retrieved 2026-10-19; Regulation (EU) 2016/679 , Art. 32(1)(a), (c), (d) · retrieved 2026-10-23 Interpretation The built-in protection of current systems meets every form we read; nobody asks a small business for a product name. Device encryption of laptops and phones is our reading of ENISA's step 6 and the VdS chapter on mobile systems: a lost laptop with personal data and without encryption is usually a breach you must report within 72 hours; with encryption it is usually a lost laptop that you note in the incident log. The example business: "in place". E4 For suppliers of software or devices: a contact for vulnerability reports and a support period for the products. Fact The Cyber Resilience Act obliges manufacturers of products with digital elements to handle vulnerabilities "for the support period", which "shall be at least five years" unless the product is expected to be in use for less; to designate "a single point of contact to enable users to communicate directly and rapidly with them, including in order to facilitate reporting on vulnerabilities", which "shall not limit such means to automated tools"; to put in place a policy on coordinated vulnerability disclosure; and to provide security updates without delay and free of charge. The Regulation applies from 11 December 2027; the duty to report actively exploited vulnerabilities applies from 11 September 2026. The Implementing Regulation asks relevant entities to track vulnerabilities and to write the handling of vulnerabilities into supplier contracts; the Directive's area (e) names "vulnerability handling and disclosure". Source: Regulation (EU) 2024/2847 (Cyber Resilience Act), Art. 13(8) and (17), Art. 14, Art. 71, Annex I Part II points 2, 5, 6 and 8, Annex II point 2; Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2690 , Annex 5.1.4(f) and 6.10; Directive (EU) 2022/2555 , Art. 21(2)(e) · retrieved 2026-10-19 Interpretation A business that only uses software answers "not applicable" and loses nothing. A business that ships devices or software already has one duty today: since 11 September 2026 it reports actively exploited vulnerabilities in its products under Article 14. The contact address and the support statement it can publish now, before the rest of the Regulation applies in December 2027; both are what customers under the Implementing Regulation must ask for. The example business installs but does not manufacture: "not applicable". E5 Router or firewall current, administrator password changed, remote administration off, a separate guest network. Fact Mannheimer asks whether the network was segmented; Markel requires firewalls at all transitions to the internet; the label's B7 asks for the manufacturer's recommended security settings and B10 whether the network is secured against unauthorised access from outside; VdS 10000 names segmentation and remote access in its network chapter; the Implementing Regulation requires configuration management, network security controls and segmentation; ENISA's step 7 is "secure your network" with firewalls and a review of remote access. The RTO must be shorter than the tolerable downtime. Multi-factor authentication (MFA). Sign-in with a second factor next to the password: an app, a security key, or as a last resort a code by SMS. Questions C2 and C3. Phishing-resistant. An authenticator that cannot be tricked by a fake page: a security key or a passkey, as ranked by NIST and CISA. Privileged account. An account with administrator rights; kept separate from the daily account (C5). Segmentation. Splitting a network so that visitors and devices that need no access cannot reach the office systems; the guest network of question E5. Backup out of reach. A copy an attacker with the office's rights cannot delete or encrypt: offline, rotated, or immutable (D1). Restore test. Restoring real data from the backup and noting date, duration and result (D2). Data processing agreement. The contract under Art. 28(3) GDPR between a controller and a processor (H2). Subcontractor. A provider your provider uses, or a provider you use for the customer's data; customers want to know of changes (H3). Audit right. The clause under which a customer may inspect or receive reports; point 5.1.4(e) of the Implementing Regulation and Art. 30(3)(e) DORA; D6 says what a small business can accept. Essential and important entity. The two classes of businesses covered by NIS 2; the customers that send questionnaires. Relevant entities. The digital providers the Implementing Regulation binds directly; in Austria, by the NISV 2026, every NIS 2 entity. Self-declaration. D1 of this toolkit; also the Austrian label's Standard level and the filing under § 33 NISG 2026, which are different documents. Significant incident. An incident that causes or can cause severe disruption or financial loss to the entity, or considerable damage to others (Art. 23(3) of the Directive). For digital providers, and in Austria for every covered entity, one criterion is a direct financial loss above 500 000 euro or 5 percent of the previous year's turnover, whichever is lower. Only a significant incident starts your customer's 24-hour clock. CSIRT. Computer security incident response team: the body that receives incident reports under NIS 2. In Austria the sector CSIRT or, if there is none, the national CSIRT (§ 34 NISG 2026); in Germany reports go to the BSI (F1). USP. The Austrian business service portal (Unternehmensserviceportal), through which covered entities register under the NISG 2026 (section 5.1). Support period. The time for which a manufacturer handles vulnerabilities of a product under the Cyber Resilience Act; at least five years, shorter where the product is expected to be in use for less (E4). Single point of contact. The manufacturer's contact for vulnerability reports, not limited to automated tools (E4). Coordinated vulnerability disclosure. The policy under which a manufacturer receives and fixes reported vulnerabilities before they are published. CVSS. A score from 0 to 10 for how severe a vulnerability is; Markel wants 8.0 and above handled without delay. Attachment number. The number D4 gives each piece of evidence that exists; D1 and D5 refer to it. Frozen version. A dated copy of the document set kept in the account; the review creates a new one. Gap. In this toolkit: a field the business fills itself, with a sentence next to it that says what the decision means and where the handbook explains it. 8 Sources All sources were read at the originals on 19 October 2026, except where the entry says otherwise. EUR-Lex and RIS texts were opened in a browser and the article text was copied from the page; PDF documents were downloaded and searched by page; the questionnaire catalogues and insurer forms were collected by web search and retrieval and spot-checked. Copies of the PDFs are kept with the project. Quotations from German sources are our translations. Passages corrected after the review of 23 October 2026 were checked again on that day, some in the copies of 19 October kept with the project; their source lines carry the date 2026-10-23. title: Datenschutz · Scutoria
main: Entwurf. Dieser Text wurde noch nicht rechtlich geprüft. Datenschutzerklärung Verantwortlicher Stefan Dallinger, Kleinpoppen, 3902 Vitis, Österreich, kontakt@scutoria.com . Angaben zum Anbieter stehen im Impressum. Grundsatz Diese Website setzt selbst ein einziges Cookie: das Sitzungs-Cookie Ihres Kundenkontos, nur wenn Sie sich anmelden, und nur so lange, wie Sie angemeldet bleiben (höchstens 30 Tage). Es ist für die Anmeldung technisch notwendig und braucht keine Einwilligung [§ 165 Abs. 3 TKG 2021, Stand prüfen]. Zusätzlich setzt die Infrastruktur unseres Hosters, Cloudflare, Inc., beim Aufruf das Cookie „__cf_bm“, um automatisierte Zugriffe zu erkennen und abzuwehren. Es enthält laut Cloudflare verschlüsselte Angaben zur Bot-Erkennung, ist keiner Kennung in unserer Website zugeordnet und verfällt nach 30 Minuten ohne Aktivität (Cloudflare, „Cloudflare Cookies“, Stand 12. Oktober 2026, abgerufen 2. November 2026). Es dient dem Schutz des Dienstes und braucht ebenfalls keine Einwilligung [§ 165 Abs. 3 TKG 2021, Stand prüfen]. Die Website verwendet keine Werbe- oder Analysedienste Dritter und lädt keine Schriften oder Skripte von fremden Servern. Welche Dienstleister Daten erhalten, steht in den folgenden Abschnitten vollständig. August 2026, Stand prüfen]; die Server-Programme laufen [auf der Infrastruktur von Cloudflare, Inc., Stand prüfen]. Ihre Daten aus Konto, Generator, Warteliste und Memo-Anforderungen liegen in einer Datenbank von Lovable Cloud [betrieben mit Supabase, Inc., Stand prüfen] in einem Rechenzentrum von Amazon Web Services in Irland (Region eu-west-1). Beim Aufruf verarbeiten diese Anbieter technisch notwendige Daten (IP-Adresse, Zeitpunkt, aufgerufene Adresse, Browserkennung) in Protokollen, um den Dienst bereitzustellen und abzusichern. Auftragsverarbeitung mit Lovable: Vertrag nach Art. 28 DSGVO, im Business-Tarif von Lovable enthalten, den Scutoria nutzt (lovable.dev/data-processing-agreement, Stand 6. November 2025). Lovable ist ein Unternehmen in den USA; soweit Daten dorthin oder in andere Länder außerhalb des EWR gelangen, geschieht das auf Grundlage der EU-Standardvertragsklauseln, die Lovable in seinen Auftragsverarbeitungsvertrag einbezieht. Dabei werden keine IP-Adresse, keine Browserkennung und kein Cookie gespeichert; die Zahlen lassen sich keiner Person zuordnen. Warteliste und Benachrichtigung Wenn Sie sich auf die Warteliste setzen, speichern wir Ihre E-Mail-Adresse, die gewählte Sprache und den Zeitpunkt Ihrer Einwilligung, um Sie einmal zu benachrichtigen, sobald das erste Produkt erhältlich ist. Die Adresse wird nach dem Versand der Benachrichtigung, spätestens nach [90 Tagen], gelöscht, sofern Sie nicht einen Newsletter bestellt haben. Einen Namen des Betriebs fragen wir nur, wenn Sie das Memo als PDF per E-Mail anfordern; er erscheint nur im PDF und wird nicht gespeichert. Wenn Sie das Memo per E-Mail anfordern, speichern wir Ihre E-Mail-Adresse, das angeforderte Memo, sein Ergebnis, die gewählte Sprache, ob Sie die Benachrichtigung über das nächste Toolkit wünschen, und den Zeitpunkt Ihrer Anforderung, um das Memo einmal als PDF zu senden, und zählen die Anforderung ohne Personenbezug. Die Adresse wird nach [90 Tagen] gelöscht, sofern Sie nicht auch die Benachrichtigung über das nächste Toolkit (siehe oben) oder einen Newsletter bestellt haben. Versand über [Brevo, Sendinblue SAS, Paris; Auftragsverarbeitung, Stand prüfen]; [falls die Kontaktliste für Memos genutzt wird: Die Adresse wird für denselben Zweck und dieselbe Dauer in einer Kontaktliste bei Brevo geführt]. Die Antworten können Namen, Telefonnummern und Anschriften enthalten, die Sie für Ihre Dokumente eingeben, zum Beispiel die verantwortliche Person und ihre Vertretung; Sie entscheiden, was Sie eingeben. Die Antworten und Dokumente bleiben für die Laufzeit der Lizenz [und zwölf Monate danach, Stand prüfen] gespeichert; danach löschen wir sie. Ihre Rechte Sie haben das Recht auf Auskunft, Berichtigung, Löschung, Einschränkung der Verarbeitung, Datenübertragbarkeit und Widerspruch, sowie das Recht, eine Einwilligung jederzeit zu widerrufen. title: Über Scutoria · Scutoria
main: So arbeiten wir Scutoria macht Informationssicherheit, Compliance und den Einsatz von KI für Betriebe ohne eigene IT-Abteilung umsetzbar. Diese Seite sagt, wie die Inhalte entstehen, was sie leisten und wo ihre Grenze liegt. Wofür Scutoria da ist Für Betriebe mit bis zu etwa fünfzig Beschäftigten, in denen die Leitung selbst entscheidet, weil es keine eigene IT- oder Sicherheitsabteilung gibt. Drei Themen gehören dabei zusammen: Sicherheit, Wirtschaft und KI. Zwei Toolkits und ein drittes in Vorbereitung, jedes aus Ihren Antworten gebaut: ein Online-Fragebogen, der die fertigen Dokumente erzeugt, ein kurzes Handbuch, das jede Entscheidung mit Quelle erklärt, Vorlagen, eine Nachweisseite und zwölf Monate Aktualisierungen. Daneben kostenlose Tools: ein paar Fragen, dann ein datiertes Memo mit den einschlägigen Artikeln. Wie wir recherchieren Jede Aussage trägt ihre Quelle: Herausgeber, Titel, Datum des Dokuments, Abrufdatum und Link. Rechtstexte lesen wir im Original, etwa im Amtsblatt der Europäischen Union oder im österreichischen Rechtsinformationssystem, nicht in Zusammenfassungen Dritter. Was sich nicht belegen lässt, heißt bei uns „nicht ermittelbar“, mit Grund. Wir schätzen nicht, runden nicht und füllen nichts plausibel auf. Wie wir mit Unsicherheit umgehen Jedes Handbuch kennzeichnet jede Aussage mit einem von vier Markern: Fakt, steht so in der genannten Quelle; Auslegung, unsere Einordnung, als solche gekennzeichnet; Unsicher, nicht abschließend geklärt, der Grund bleibt sichtbar; Lücke, fehlt und wird benannt, nicht gefüllt. Jedes Produkt endet mit seinen Quellen und seinen offenen Punkten. Nichts verschwindet stillschweigend im Fließtext. Wie wir aktualisieren Aktualisierungen innerhalb eines Lizenzjahres erscheinen in Ihrem Konto, ohne dass Sie etwas tun müssen; die Versionszeile auf jeder Seite zeigt den Stand. Einrichtungsanleitungen tragen das Datum der gezeigten Oberfläche, weil jede Oberfläche veraltet. Tools nennen den Stand ihrer Quellen auf der Seite. Wie wir Werkzeuge einsetzen Die Inhalte entstehen KI-gestützt und werden vor der Veröffentlichung von Menschen geprüft: Quellen gegengelesen, Zahlen und Fristen nachgeschlagen, offene Punkte benannt. Was ein Werkzeug nicht belegen kann, kommt nicht in ein Produkt. Was wir nicht tun Wir beraten nicht und wir vertreten nicht. Die Produkte sind Ratgeber, keine rechtlich verbindlichen Dokumente, und ersetzen keine Prüfung des Einzelfalls. Kein Tool stellt fest, ob eine Vorschrift für einen bestimmten Betrieb gilt, und keines bewertet Produkte einzelner Anbieter. Wer dahintersteht Scutoria ist ein kleines Unternehmen mit Sitz in Österreich. Die Angaben zum Anbieter stehen im Impressum. Fragen zu Zugang, Rechnung oder Inhalt erreichen uns unter kontakt@scutoria.com und werden innerhalb von zwei Werktagen beantwortet. Quellenbasiert. Keine Rechtsberatung. „Stand prüfen“ heißt bei uns: Datum und Quelle stehen dabei, die Prüfung im Einzelfall bleibt Ihre.

Wo die Regeln sich unterscheiden, sagen wir es. 2. Leistung Scutoria verkauft Jahreslizenzen für digitale Produkte („Toolkits“). Eine Lizenz umfasst für zwölf Monate ab Kauf: den Online-Fragebogen (Generator), die daraus erzeugten Dokumente als PDF und DOCX, das zugehörige Handbuch, die Vorlagen, die Nachweisseite, das Kundenkonto mit Nachweisordner und alle Aktualisierungen des Produkts in dieser Zeit. Der genaue Umfang steht auf der Produktseite zum Zeitpunkt der Bestellung. Die Produkte sind Ratgeber und Vorlagen. Sie sind keine Rechtsberatung, kein Zertifikat und keine Bestätigung, dass ein Betrieb eine Vorschrift erfüllt. 3. Bestellung und Vertragsschluss Die Darstellung der Produkte ist kein verbindliches Angebot. Mit „Jahreslizenz kaufen“ gelangen Sie auf die Zahlungsseite von Stripe; mit dem Klick auf die Zahlungsschaltfläche dort („Bezahlen“) geben Sie ein verbindliches Angebot ab [Beschriftung der Schaltfläche nach § 8 Abs. 2 FAGG, Stand prüfen]. Der Vertrag kommt zustande, wenn Scutoria die Bestellung per E-Mail bestätigt und den Zugang bereitstellt. Die Zahlung wird über Stripe abgewickelt (Stripe Payments Europe, Ltd., Dublin). Vertragssprachen sind Deutsch und Englisch; [bei Abweichungen gilt die deutsche Fassung, Stand prüfen]. 4. Preise und Zahlung Alle Preise in Euro. [Die Preise verstehen sich inklusive Umsatzsteuer.] oder [Scutoria ist Kleinunternehmer gemäß § 6 Abs. 1 Z 27 UStG; Umsatzsteuer wird nicht ausgewiesen.] Festlegung nach Auskunft des Steuerberaters. Für Unternehmer mit Sitz in einem anderen EU-Mitgliedstaat und gültiger UID gilt [das Reverse-Charge-Verfahren, Stand prüfen]. Zahlungsarten sind die in der Kasse angebotenen, etwa Karte und SEPA-Lastschrift, je nach Land. Die Rechnung kommt per E-Mail. 5. Zugang und Lieferung Der Zugang wird nach Zahlungseingang sofort bereitgestellt: per E-Mail mit persönlichem Link und im Kundenkonto. Mit der Bereitstellung gilt die Lieferung als erfolgt. 6. Widerrufsrecht für Verbraucher Verbraucher haben ein vierzehntägiges Widerrufsrecht; Einzelheiten stehen in der Widerrufsbelehrung. Bei digitalen Inhalten erlischt es, wenn Sie vor Ablauf der Frist ausdrücklich zustimmen, dass die Lieferung sofort beginnt, und bestätigen, dass Sie damit Ihr Widerrufsrecht verlieren (§ 18 Abs. 1 Z 11 FAGG). Diese Zustimmung holt die Kasse ein. Unternehmer haben kein Widerrufsrecht. 7. Nutzungsrecht Die Lizenz gilt für einen Betrieb (ein Unternehmen) und seine Beschäftigten. Sie dürfen die erzeugten Dokumente und Vorlagen für diesen Betrieb anpassen, intern verwenden, ausdrucken und Kunden, Versicherern oder Behörden vorlegen. Nicht erlaubt sind die Weitergabe oder der Weiterverkauf der Produkte, die Nutzung für mehrere Betriebe, die Nutzung durch Berater für deren Kunden ohne gesonderte Vereinbarung und die Veröffentlichung des Handbuchs. 8. Vor dem Ablauf erhalten Sie eine Erinnerung; die Verlängerung ist ein neuer Kauf. Nach Ablauf bleiben die bis dahin erzeugten Dokumente [zwölf weitere Monate, Stand prüfen] im Konto abrufbar; Generator und Aktualisierungen stehen dann nicht mehr zur Verfügung. 9. Ein Anspruch auf einen bestimmten Zeitpunkt der Aktualisierung besteht nicht. 10. Gewährleistung und Haftung Es gilt die gesetzliche Gewährleistung. Scutoria haftet für Vorsatz und grobe Fahrlässigkeit sowie für Personenschäden. Gegenüber Unternehmern ist die Haftung für leichte Fahrlässigkeit ausgeschlossen, ausgenommen Personenschäden. Sie können Ihr Konto jederzeit löschen lassen; gesetzliche Aufbewahrungspflichten für Rechnungsdaten bleiben bestehen. 12. Für Verbraucher gelten die gesetzlichen Gerichtsstände; zwingende Verbraucherschutzvorschriften ihres Wohnsitzstaates bleiben unberührt. 13.
